dimension_grades.evidence: The entire draft is written in narrative prose paragraphs — 'The team has made really solid progress this week on the Atlas migration. After several productive working sessions...' — with no bullet points anywhere.
There are no bullet points in the draft; all information is conveyed in multi-sentence prose paragraphs.

The payment processor issue is mentioned in 'Blockers and Challenges' and again in 'Next Steps' ('we plan to continue debugging the payment processor integration'); CI/CD pipeline issues also appear in both sections.
A 'Broader Context' section exists solely to discuss hiring freeze and burnout concerns, which could be folded into Blockers or Next Steps rather than standing as its own section.
The first line after the greeting is 'I hope this message finds you well and that you had a great weekend,' which is context-setting pleasantry, not a status summary.
There is no single summary sentence capturing wins and timeline shifts; wins and blockers are buried in separate paragraphs deep in the email.
There is no upfront signal about whether action is needed; the escalation recommendation ('flag both of these to the VP') appears buried in the Blockers section.
There is no summary line at all — labeled or unlabeled — at the top of the email.

The draft uses alarm language throughout: 'significant setback,' 'serious concern,' 'scrambling,' 'failed during end-to-end testing,' 'real headache,' and 'I'm not confident we'll be able to resolve this.'
The Next Steps section states 'it's hard to say exactly when we'll know more' about the payment processor, leaving timeline impact entirely vague.
No specific date or timeframe is given for when the resolution path will be clear; the draft only says they 'hope to have a clearer picture' without specifying when.
Rather than signaling no escalation is needed, the draft explicitly recommends escalation: 'I'd recommend we flag both of these to the VP sooner rather than later.'
The draft contains no internet-style abbreviations or casual shorthand labels; it errs toward formal prose throughout.

The closing reads 'Please don't hesitate to reach out if you'd like to set up time to discuss any of this in greater detail. I'm happy to put together a more comprehensive briefing document,' which is overly formal and stiff rather than approachable.

The draft uses verbose, formal prose with lengthy pleasantries and alarm language that would likely land poorly with a director reading on mobile between meetings, showing no calibration to the recipient's communication style.
